sentences.text: Tyrannosaurus possessed short but unusually powerful forelimbs with two clawed digits, contrasting sharply with its massive hind limbs.
While the most complete specimen measures 12.3 to 12.4 meters in length, modern estimates suggest the animal could reach 13 meters long, 3.7 to 4 meters high at the hips, and weigh 8.8 tons.

The Bucky specimen is the first Tyrannosaurus skeleton found to preserve a furcula, or wishbone, while the Stan skeleton is the second most complete, with 199 recovered bones representing 70% of the total.
A tooth now identified as Tyrannosaurus rex was found in July 1874 by Peter T. Dotson near Golden, Colorado, in the Denver Formation.

In 1892, Edward Drinker Cope named Manospondylus gigas based on two vertebral fragments he found, initially believing them to be from a ceratopsid dinosaur, until the Black Hills Institute found around 10% of a Tyrannosaurus skeleton at a site potentially linked to that locality in June 2000.
The genus Tyrannosaurus was formally described by Osborn in 1905.
Tyrannosaurus rex was likely an apex predator that preyed on hadrosaurs, juvenile ceratopsians, ankylosaurs, and possibly sauropods, though some experts suggest it was primarily a scavenger.

A 2026 study based on bone histology suggests Tyrannosaurus had a more gradual annual growth rate and a prolonged subadult stage than previously thought, while another 2026 study indicates its foot-strike patterns were similar to those of ostriches.

The type species of the genus Tyrannosaurus is Tyrannosaurus rex. Tyrannosaurids were once thought to be descendants of megalosaurs and carnosaurs but were later reclassified with the smaller coelurosaurs, and many phylogenetic analyses have identified Tarbosaurus bataar as the sister taxon of Tyrannosaurus.
A potential species T. mcraeensis was proposed by Dalman et al. in 2024.

Tyrannosaurus lived during the late Cretaceous period, between 72 and 66 million years ago, in what is now North America, with a genus time range from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian stages (83.6 to 66 million years ago).

Tyrannosaurs began as small theropods, with at least some becoming larger by the Early Cretaceous, and fossils range from the Late Cretaceous (late Maastrichtian) to a possible record from the middle Campanian.

There is a scientific debate regarding the Jane skeleton, which was initially thought to be a pygmy tyrannosaurid (Nanotyrannus) but is now re-described as the holotype of N. lethaeus, though some researchers still consider it a juvenile T. rex.

A 2016 study suggests Tyrannosaurus may have been an immigrant from Asia and a possible descendant of Tarbosaurus, while there is a debate among paleontologists regarding whether Tarbosaurus bataar should be classified as a distinct genus or as a species within Tyrannosaurus.
The validity of recently discovered species like T. mcraeensis is considered contentious.
